cards.title: Name as the Core Positioning Decision
cards.summary: The product or brand name is the single most important marketing decision because it is the hook that hangs the brand on a ladder in the prospect's mind.
cards.use_when: Naming a new product, brand, SKU or storefront, or deciding whether to rename an existing product line.
steps: Treat the name as the first positioning act, not a cosmetic label. The source (Ries & Trout) argues that in an overcommunicated market the name is the single most important marketing decision, because the mind stores a product by its name.
Choose a name that begins the positioning process: pick a name that telegraphs the product's major benefit, in the way Head & Shoulders signals dandruff care and DieHard signals long battery life.
For ecommerce listings, aim for a name that makes the benefit legible in the search result, the cart line and the ad headline — where you have seconds, not a salesperson.
Avoid names that are lazy, do-nothing or purely internal (project codes, initials, founder surnames) unless the brand is already first and famous in the category.
Remember that Shakespeare was wrong according to the source: a rose by any other name would not smell as sweet, because people see and smell what they expect to.
Run a sounding test before committing to a name you plan to say in video, podcast ads or voice search.
caveats: The source is opinionated and dated; the core claim is a positioning argument, not a measured benchmark.
Benefit-led names risk becoming generic if too close to the category (see separate card on that trap).

cards.title: Descriptive Names Beat Coined Names — Unless You're First
cards.summary: Pick a name that nearly describes the benefit rather than a meaningless coined word, because only a genuine first mover can afford an empty name.
cards.use_when: Deciding between a descriptive name (e.g. Soy Butter, Spray 'n Wash) and a coined or abstract brand name for a new product or store line.
steps: Prefer common descriptive words that say what the product does, in the tradition of Spray 'n Wash and DieHard; these block me-too competitors from muscling into your territory.
Reserve coined, meaningless names (the source's examples: Kodak, Keds, Kleenex) for the case where you are first into the mind with an absolutely new product that millions will want.

Understand that Coca-Cola, Kodak and Xerox succeeded because they were first in their categories, not because the names were invented; the source calls this the Charles Lindbergh syndrome — get in first and any name works.

For an ecommerce store launching a familiar category (supplements, cookware, apparel basics), use a benefit-descriptive naming pattern rather than abstract invented words, since you are not likely to be first.
Check letter-frequency as a rough guide: the most common English initial letters are S, C, P, A and T, and the least common are X, Z, Y, Q and K — a name starting with X is far harder to recall.
caveats: The source's claim that only first-movers can afford coined names is a heuristic, not a tested rule.
Descriptive names invite trademark trouble and category substitution (Lite problem).
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Don't Let a Name Become Generic
cards.summary: A name should point to your benefit without sliding all the way into a generic category word, or you lose exclusive rights to it.
cards.use_when: Naming or trademarking a launch SKU, deciding whether to coin a new word for a new product format, or reviewing a product name that has become a category catch-all.
steps: Aim for a name that is almost-but-not-quite generic, the way the source describes choosing like driving a racing car — you must take chances and occasionally spin out.

Watch the cautionary case of 'Lite beer from Miller': the press and public shortened it to 'Miller Lite,' and Miller lost exclusive rights to 'light' or its phonetic equivalent as a trademark for beer.

If your name is already a category word (e.g. a store brand literally called 'Vitamin C'), the source's warning applies at scale: you have made it easy for competitors to sell under the same literal label.
When a coined name is genuinely warranted, keep it distinguishable: a strong, generic-like but not-generic name blocks me-too competitors, according to the source.
Consult trademark counsel before launch on any name that reads as a category description; the source notes trademark lawyers prefer coined marks like Kodak and Xerox.
caveats: Choice of name is a trade-off: too abstract and the prospect learns nothing; too descriptive and you lose the mark.
Legal standards vary by jurisdiction and category; get current local advice.

cards.title: Audit Existing Names for Obsolescence and Confusion
cards.summary: Names decay as products and markets change; audit the ladder to spot names that mislead or overlap with competitors.
cards.use_when: Portfolio review: assessing whether a legacy brand or product name still communicates the current offer, or whether a rename is warranted.
steps: Check the ladder position, not the aesthetics. The source's Eastern Airlines case: a regional name placed Eastern in the same mental bracket as Piedmont and Ozark, not the national carriers.
Look for names that no longer match what the product does: United Shoe Machinery, RCA and Esquire all outgrew or lost the thing their name meant.

Watch for name confusion with a larger competitor. In the source's famous case, B. F. Goodrich was the first to market steel-belted radials in the U.S., yet 56% of buyers named Goodyear (which didn't make them domestically) versus 47% who named Goodrich.
Check the Toledo triplet / Continental confusion problem: when multiple brands share a common word, prospect research cannot distinguish them; use a name test to measure misattribution.

Recall that names can carry hidden devalued meaning (the source's example of 'margarine' hiding its soy origin), so test whether the current name withholds or misrepresents what the product actually is.

Assess whether a rename will actually help. The source says most companies refuse to change because they believe 'our customers and employees would never accept a new name' — but cites Uniroyal, Eaton, Mobil and Exxon as successful renames.
caveats: Rename case studies are retrospective examples, not guarantees of improved sales.
Goodrich opted to keep the name and effectively told customers it was their problem to remember it — a defensible but expensive choice.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Test Names and Headlines for Sound, Not Just Look
cards.summary: The mind processes words aurally, so evaluate names, slogans and headlines by how they sound, especially for future voice and podcast channels.
cards.use_when: Choosing a store or product name, writing ad headlines or slogans, or preparing a brand name for voice search and audio advertising.
steps: Read names and headlines aloud before committing; if a name sounds bad, it will feel bad even in print, because the brain translates letters into sound.
Apply the phonetic shorthand test: RCA (3 syllables) works versus Radio Corporation of America (12); GE works versus General Electric (6); but Ford is rarely FM because Ford is already one syllable.
For ecommerce, test the name in spoken contexts — audio ads, video UGC, voice search queries — not just in a logo lockup, since ads are increasingly heard.
Design ad copy for 'radio first' as the source suggests, then adapt to print and display, because the primal medium is sound.
Watch name collisions that only appear in written form: USM's 'US' doesn't stand for anything, so it sorts into the phone-book front matter where no one looks.
caveats: Phonetic shorthand rules were developed in an era dominated by radio and print; streaming and app search change the retrieval rules but not the value of a pronounceable name.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Initials and Acronyms Are a Shortcut Trap
cards.summary: Companies copy IBM's initials and mistake cause for effect — initials work only after a name is already famous.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to brand a new store line, private label or acquisition sub-brand with initials or an acronym, or reviewing a corporate rebrand.
steps: Apply the cause-and-effect test: the source argues that IBM got rich and famous first (the cause), which made its initials widely understood (the effect). Reversing the sequence does not work.

Take the source's measured example with caution: a Business Week subscriber survey found average awareness of 'initial' companies at 49% versus 68% for a matched group of 'name' companies, a 19-point gap.
If you inherit an initial name, verify there is a buried, well-known original name for the initials to trigger; otherwise the mind gets nothing back when it reads the letters.
Check the telephone-directory (or search-results) behavior of an initial name: MCI sorts 48 pages away from where customers look, and competes with several other MCI-containing companies.

Prefer a shortened name with phonetic gain over initials. The source contrasts Pan Am (2 syllables, better than PAA) with TWA, where 'Trans World' (2 syllables) is shorter and clearer than the T-Double-U-A it uses.
Reserve initials for brands that are already household-level famous; even the source concedes ITT and NCR work only because they were well known before they went initial.
caveats: The 49%/68% awareness survey is a single source study and should be read as illustrative, not a benchmark for your category.
Some acronyms are deliberate and work as names (CARE, MADD, Fiat, Sabena), so the rule is 'do the initials add phonetic or mnemonic value?' not 'never abbreviate'.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Line Extension Blurs a Hard-Won Position
cards.summary: Hanging a known name on a new category fails because the brand name is a surrogate for the original product in the prospect's mind.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to launch a new product or category under the existing hero brand name versus creating a new brand or sub-brand, e.g. an existing supplement brand moving into skincare.
steps: Apply the teeter-totter principle: one name cannot stand for two distinctly different products; when one goes up, the other goes down.

Recall the source's Bayer case: 'Bayer nonaspirin' never took more than a tiny share of the acetaminophen market, and each extension — Bayer timed-release aspirin, Bayer decongestant cold tablets — undercut the core aspirin position.
Recall Dial: a large share of the soap market and a very small share of the deodorant market after extending the Dial name.
Recall Protein 21: from a 13% share of shampoo to 2% after launching hairspray, conditioner and Protein 29 for men.
For ecommerce, decide pre-launch whether a new product requires a new mental ladder. If the source's logic holds, a genuinely new product needs a new ladder and therefore a new name.
Weigh the inside-out argument ('our customers know us, they'll accept it, we'll save marketing dollars') against the outside-in view (the prospect thinks in products, not companies).
caveats: The source argues that Procter & Gamble's no-house-name strategy beat Colgate-Palmolive (roughly twice the business and five times the profit) — a historical comparison, not a guaranteed operating rule.
There are exceptions: some brands extend successfully when the new product is genuinely within the same ladder. Run a name-fit test before launching.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Use a Distinctly Named Hero SKU to Hold a Feature
cards.summary: Give a product a name that carries the benefit, so the customer has a hook to hang attributes on.
cards.use_when: Naming a flagship SKU or private-label item where you want one benefit to be remembered, e.g. an extended-life battery, a durability claim, or a specific food benefit.
steps: Name the product for the benefit, not the retailer. In the source's example, the DieHard battery gave the buyer a mental hook for 'long-lasting', while the JCPenney battery gave a weak hook for the 'never needs water' feature.

Accept the trade-off: the DieHard name makes it hard to remember it is only sold at Sears, but the source argues it is better to establish the position in the prospect's mind first and solve the retail connection later.
For a store brand, consider whether your retail name is strong enough to hold a functional claim, or whether a differentiated product brand fits the ladder better.
When naming a bundle or kit, choose a name that conveys the primary benefit rather than a house name that simply identifies who made it.
Recognize that 'the obvious name is not always the best name'; the source warns that obvious, internal-logic names are a barrier to success.
caveats: Sears' retail-connection problem is real; a great name cannot fix distribution customers cannot easily reach.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: New Product, New Ladder, New Name
cards.summary: A truly new product cannot live on a famous name because the famous name occupies a sharply defined rung of a different ladder.
cards.use_when: Launching a new product line in a new category under a company that already owns a position in another category.
steps: Ask what the existing brand name stands for in the prospect's mind. If the answer is a specific product (Xerox means copier), the name cannot also mean a new category.

Recall the Xerox experiment: Xerox bought Scientific Data Systems and renamed it Xerox Data Systems; the ad line 'This Xerox machine can't make a copy' signals the trap, and the company folded the computer operation with an additional $84.4 million write-off.
Also recall Heinz: it made Heinz mean ketchup, gaining the No. 1 ketchup position, while losing pickle leadership to Vlasic — the other end of the teeter-totter.
Before launch, ask whether you are prepared to make the hero name mean the new thing. If the answer is no, launch under a new dedicated name.
Be honest about the corporate-ego problem: the source observes that telling GE not to put GE on a new product is very difficult, which is exactly why the wrong decisions get made.
caveats: This is the source's opinion, illustrated through historical cases; not every extension fails.
Sub-brand naming can capture some, but not all, of the separation benefits described.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Use Negative Names to Polarize Instead of Hide
cards.summary: When a product's origin is hidden, prospects suspect a problem; a proudly descriptive name builds 'pride of origin' and a long-term positioning campaign.
cards.use_when: Naming or renaming a product whose origin or formulation is unfamiliar to buyers — alternative ingredients, plant-based or lab-made goods, or a product seen as an imitation.
steps: Bring the product out of the closet by deliberately naming the origin, as in the source's prescription that margarine should have been called 'soy butter' rather than hiding its source.

The source's logic: because the origin of margarine is hidden, the prospect assumes something is wrong with it; a name that names the source allows a long-term program selling the advantages of soy butter versus cow butter.

Apply the same principle to corn sweeteners, which the source says were hampered by names like 'high-fructose corn syrup'; renaming to 'corn sugars' let corn stand on equal footing with cane and beet.
For an ecommerce store selling a product category that suffers from an imitation perception, build the origin into the brand name and the PDP headline rather than burying it in the 'About' section.

When fighting an entrenched competitor term (the source cites 'fair trade' laws), do not try to rename the competition — that only confuses the audience. Turn the name around: 'Fair to the trade, but unfair to the consumer.'
caveats: Renaming an entrenched concept early — before the powerful name takes root — is much more effective than late; the source notes 'price maintenance' as a blocking strategy would probably have worked only early.
Some origin words carry stigma the brand may not be able to neutralize; validate with real customer language before committing.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Protect a Position You Already Own
cards.summary: A brand that owns a category position (Kleenex, Hertz, Cadillac, Xerox) holds enormous long-term value; do not spend it on a different category.
cards.use_when: Portfolio and pricing decisions when a hero brand or hero SKU is being considered as a vehicle for a new offer, bundle or adjacent category.
steps: Identify the position the name actually owns — the generic substitute customers use in speech ('hand me a Kleenex', 'get me a Xerox copy').
Note that generic-strong brands can promote the category, not the brand ('Coffee keeps you awake? Drink Sanka'), which is an efficiency advantage worth protecting.
Beware of teaching the prospect that your brand is 'nothing but a brand name'. Each line extension, according to the source, destroys the illusion that the brand is a superior form of the product.
For subscription and replenishment stores, keep the hero position on the hero product and avoid using it as a banner for consumables of a different job-to-be-done.
If you must grow into a new category, create a new brand or an explicitly distinct sub-brand rather than diluting the core name.
caveats: The source is strongly anti-extension; some brands do extend profitably, so treat this as a risk framework rather than an absolute ban.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Spend Publicity Like a Budget, Not a Habit
cards.summary: Anonymity is an easily squandered resource; a lesser-known product gains far more from publicity than a famous one does.
cards.use_when: Planning a PR push, press outreach or influencer campaign for a new store, brand or hero product, and deciding when to use your best story.
steps: Conserve anonymity until you are ready to spend it, then spend it big, keeping the objective on a position in the prospect's mind rather than on coverage for its own sake.
Recognize that media hunger is for the new and fresh face; an unknown company with an unknown product has more to gain from publicity than a well-known company with an established product.
Note the source's caution that nothing kills the publicity potential of a product quite as much as a cover story in a national magazine — repeated exposure without a purpose burns the asset.
For an ecommerce launch, time the one big reveal around the moment a purchase decision is actually possible (site live, inventory ready), not months before.
Use the momentum of a media moment to convert — landing page, offer and stock — rather than treating coverage as the goal.
caveats: The source treats publicity as finite, which may understate the compounding effect of a well-run content channel.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Use House Names and Separate Names According to Provenance
cards.summary: How a product was created (internal development vs. acquisition) historically drives naming strategy, but the prospect's mind should be the deciding factor.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether an acquired brand or a newly developed product should carry the parent store/brand name, after an acquisition or a category expansion.
steps: Know the pattern the source describes: internally developed products usually get the corporate name (General Electric computers), while acquired products usually keep their name (Hertz under RCA, Avis under ITT) — though Xerox broke the pattern by renaming Scientific Data Systems.
Treat the pattern as a default born of corporate ego, not as a decision rule derived from the customer's mind.
For an ecommerce operator buying a DTC brand, do not automatically rename the acquired brand to the parent; consider whether the acquired name holds a distinct position the parent name cannot serve.
If the parent name clearly dominates in search, subscription recognition or ad efficiency, weigh a deliberate rename against the position the acquired name already owns.
Account for conglomerate logic honestly: the source credits conglomerates with funding competition, but that business benefit does not by itself justify a naming decision.
caveats: The source's naming analysis is drawn from large industrial and packaged-goods history; small ecommerce portfolios may have different trade-offs.
cards.source_name: Positioning_ The Battle for Your Mind_ The Battle for Your Mind (1).docx

cards.title: Position Against the Future, Not the Past, When Renaming
cards.summary: When a name is obsolete, a foot-in-the-past abbreviation freezes it; a clean new name can reposition the whole company.
cards.use_when: Renaming a store, a legacy product line, or a brand after a pivot, product obsolescence or a merger.
steps: Diagnose the obsolescence honestly: U.S. Rubber sold many non-rubber products, Eaton Yale & Towne was a merger with a complicated name, and Socony-Mobil was saddled with a Standard Oil legacy name.
Do not take the easy abbreviation route; the source calls USR Corporation, EY&T Company and SM Inc. three marketing monstrosities.
Adopt a clean new name rather than initials. Uniroyal, Eaton and Mobil came from 'forgetting the past' and positioning against the future.
Expect a transitional cost but note the source's claim that there is only negative equity in a bad name — when the name is bad, things tend to get worse.
Ask the same question about a store that started in one category: is the store name now a USM-style liability, and would a name change produce a cleaner position?
caveats: Renaming is rare in practice because companies believe they have too much equity in the current name; the source counter-cites Olin, Mobil, Uniroyal, Xerox and Exxon as companies that made the change work.
